The placement

I completed my BS internship at The Character Schooling System, a private school in Shahdadpur, at its Shahbaz Khan Campus. I started on 11 September and finished on 23 October, completing all 80 internship hours in about six weeks of classes. I worked under the school principal as my institution supervisor, with a mentor teacher beside me in the building.

the journey

From Day I to the last bell

Day I

Observation: the introductory class

I started by watching and introducing myself. On the board: “I am Moomal”, plus the first lessons on he, his, him, she and her, and why we say “I study”, not “I am study”.

Grammar

Parts of Speech: all 8 at a glance

Noun, pronoun, verb, adverb, adjective, preposition, conjunction and interjection. I paired each with a one-line meaning and a quick example sentence so students could spot them in the wild.

Grammar

Tenses: 12 of them, built from three things

Subjects, helping verbs and the verb forms (eat, ate, eaten, eating). Breaking tenses into those building blocks made the “12” feel less scary.

Sentences

Active voice: subject, verb, object

Students came up to the board and labelled the subject and object themselves.

Words

Vocabulary with meanings in Urdu

Word, meaning, synonyms and antonyms, with Urdu meanings beside each English word so nobody was left behind. We also played prefix and suffix games, and a Mystery Word Challenge with clues.

Reading & writing

Writing about the 2022 floods

A short passage where students circled and corrected the key words, then wrote their own versions in their notebooks.

reflective log

Week by week, in my own words

Tap a week to open it. These are the small things I noticed, fixed and felt along the way.

Week 1Standing at the back, taking it all in

My first day was an observation class. I watched how the room worked, learned a few names and wrote my own introduction on the board. I was nervous, but the students were polite and curious, and that settled me. What I learned: a calm voice and a clear board matter more than speed. By the end of the day I was itching to teach, not just watch.

ObservationIntroductionhe · his · him
Week 2Finding my voice

This was my first real week at the board. I taught the eight parts of speech with one-line meanings, a little Urdu where it helped, and silly examples like losing a teacher’s marker and pen. I spoke too fast at first. What I learned: asking students for their own sentences slowed me down and woke the whole room up.

Parts of speechExamplesUrdu support
Week 3Making tenses less scary

Twelve tenses sounded huge, so I broke them into three things: subjects, helping verbs (am, is, are, has, have) and verb forms like eat, ate, eaten. Once the pieces were on the board, the big topic felt doable. What I learned: never start with the names of the tenses. Start with the small blocks and let students build upward.

12 tensesHelping verbsVerb forms
Week 4Handing over the marker

We moved to active and passive voice, using simple sentences like “I write a letter” to find the subject, verb and object. The best moment came when students walked up and labelled the sentences themselves. What I learned: they understood faster from each other’s mistakes than from my explanation, so I started talking less.

Active voiceSubject · verb · objectStudent turns
Week 5Words that stick

This week was vocabulary: word, meaning in Urdu, synonyms and antonyms, then prefix and suffix team games with words like replay, hopeful, dislike and fearless. What I learned: a word learned in a game stays in memory longer than a word copied from the board. Students asked for “one more round”, my favourite compliment.

VocabularySynonyms · antonymsPrefix · suffix
Week 6The final stretch

The last week had the Mystery Word Challenge, where students guessed words from riddles, and a passage on the 2022 floods where we circled and corrected key words together. On 23 October I finished my 80th hour, tired, proud and a little sad to leave. What I learned: teaching is mostly listening, and the best lesson plan is one that leaves room for the students.

Mystery Word Challenge2022 floods passageLast day

Month by month

The first weeks · from 11 September
Learning the room

Grades 5, 6, 7 and 8

The first weeks were about trust. I went from a nervous observer to someone students looked at when they had a question. I learned their names, found my pace and discovered that grammar sticks when it is built from small, friendly pieces. I made mistakes (too fast, too much talking) and fixed most of them by listening to the class.

The final stretch · until 23 October
80 / 80 hours

Completed from 11 September to 23 October

Later I stopped planning around my notes and started planning around the students. We played the Mystery Word Challenge, wrote about the 2022 floods, and kept handing the marker to students. I finished all 80 hours with more patience, simpler explanations and real confidence in front of a class.

reflection

What I take with me

Day I felt like a fresh start: I had to learn names, find my voice and stop over-explaining. By the end I was planning around what students actually needed, using simple examples, a little Urdu where it helped, and handing the marker over so they could think out loud. Teaching English taught me more about English than any exam.
